name: Cancer and the life of a cell
about: Every cell lives through the same stages: it rests or grows, copies its DNA and divides, passes checkpoints, meets toxins and damage, ages, and is meant to die and be cleared. Cancer starts when a cell slips past these controls. Genes are placed on the stage they act in, from Gene Ontology, and kept when Open Targets links them to cancer.
rule: Gene Ontology stage genes with an Open Targets cancer score ≥ 0.3, plus genes with human genetic evidence ≥ 0.5 for a cancer

mechanisms.name: Growth signals
mechanisms.about: Growth-factor receptors and the RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT relays that tell a cell to divide.
mechanisms.explain: Growth factors bind receptors on the surface (EGFR, ERBB2, FGFR, KIT), which pass the signal through RAS, RAF and MAPK, or PI3K, AKT and mTOR, to switch on the genes for division. PTEN and NF1 are brakes on these relays. A relay stuck on (a more active oncogene) or a brake lost (a less active PTEN or NF1) lets a cell divide without being told to.

mechanisms.name: Resting and staying in place
mechanisms.about: Quiescence, and the cell–cell junctions and adhesion that hold a cell in its tissue.
mechanisms.explain: Most cells in an adult are resting, held in their place by junctions with their neighbours (cadherins such as CDH1, and catenins). Contact with neighbours also tells a cell to stop dividing. Losing these contacts is an early step towards invasion; inherited CDH1 loss causes stomach and breast cancer.

mechanisms.name: Copying the DNA
mechanisms.explain: In S phase the whole genome is copied once. Polymerases with proofreading (POLE, POLD1) and the licensing system that stops a second round make it accurate. Weaker proofreading leaves more mutations behind in every division.

mechanisms.name: Dividing
mechanisms.about: Moving through the phases, separating the chromosomes and splitting the cell.
mechanisms.explain: Cyclins and CDKs move the cell from phase to phase, and RB1 holds the gate at G1 until the cell is ready. In mitosis the chromosomes are attached to the spindle and pulled apart. Losing RB1 or the CDK inhibitors (CDKN2A) lets cells cycle unchecked; missegregation gives daughter cells the wrong number of chromosomes.

mechanisms.name: Checkpoints
mechanisms.about: DNA-damage, replication and spindle checkpoints that pause the cycle.
mechanisms.explain: ATM and ATR sense broken or stalled DNA and, through CHEK1, CHEK2 and p53 (TP53), stop the cycle until it is repaired, or send the cell to die. The spindle checkpoint (BUB1, MAD2) holds division until every chromosome is attached. These are the guards cancer most often disables: TP53 is mutated in about half of all tumours, and inherited CHEK2 and ATM variants raise breast and prostate cancer risk.

mechanisms.name: Clearing toxins
mechanisms.about: Phase I and II enzymes that activate and neutralise foreign chemicals: CYPs, GSTs, NAT2, UGTs.
mechanisms.explain: Phase I enzymes (CYP1A1, CYP1B1, CYP2E1) make foreign chemicals easier to remove, but often make them more reactive first; phase II enzymes (GSTM1, GSTP1, NAT2, UGTs) attach a tag that neutralises and clears them. The balance between the two decides how much of a carcinogen from smoke, grilled meat or solvents reaches DNA. Slow NAT2 and missing GSTM1 are the classic examples, raising bladder cancer risk in smokers.

mechanisms.name: Oxidative stress
mechanisms.about: Neutralising reactive oxygen and the response to it.
mechanisms.explain: Using oxygen for energy leaks superoxide and peroxide, which damage DNA, fats and proteins. SOD2, catalase, glutathione peroxidases and NRF2 (NFE2L2) neutralise them. Weaker defences mean more oxidative DNA damage over time.

mechanisms.name: DNA repair
mechanisms.about: Mismatch, base and nucleotide excision, and double-strand break repair.
mechanisms.explain: Different systems fix different damage: mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) corrects copying errors, base excision (OGG1, MUTYH) fixes oxidised bases, nucleotide excision (XPC, ERCC2) removes UV and chemical damage, and homologous recombination (BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2) repairs double-strand breaks. Inherited loss of one copy is the cause of Lynch syndrome and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer; common variants have small effects.

mechanisms.name: Telomeres
mechanisms.about: Keeping the chromosome ends long: telomerase and the shelterin cap.
mechanisms.explain: Telomeres cap the chromosome ends and shorten with each division, which limits how often a cell can divide. Telomerase (TERT, TERC) rebuilds them in stem cells. Cancers switch telomerase back on to divide forever; TERT variants are among the strongest common risk loci for many cancers, and long telomeres raise risk for some.

mechanisms.name: Senescence
mechanisms.about: The permanent stop that ageing or damaged cells enter.
mechanisms.explain: When telomeres run short or damage persists, p53, p21 (CDKN1A) and p16 (CDKN2A) put the cell into permanent arrest. This is a barrier against cancer, but senescent cells also release inflammatory signals that, over the years, can feed the growth of nearby cells.

mechanisms.name: Programmed death
mechanisms.about: The internal (mitochondrial) and external (death receptor) routes to apoptosis.
mechanisms.explain: A cell too damaged to save dismantles itself. In the internal route p53 and BH3 proteins open the mitochondria (BAX, BAK) against the guards BCL2 and MCL1, releasing cytochrome c to start the caspases. In the external route death receptors (FAS, TNFRSF10) start them from outside. Tumours often raise BCL2 or lose BAX to survive.

mechanisms.name: Immune clearance
mechanisms.about: Showing protein fragments on MHC class I, and the T and NK cells that kill abnormal cells.
mechanisms.explain: Every cell shows fragments of its proteins on MHC class I (HLA, B2M, TAP1). Cytotoxic T cells recognise abnormal fragments from mutated proteins, and NK cells kill cells that hide their MHC. Tumours escape by losing B2M or HLA, or by raising PD-L1, which is what immunotherapy reverses.

mechanisms.name: Invasion and new blood vessels
mechanisms.about: Epithelial–mesenchymal transition, which lets a cell break loose, and angiogenesis, which feeds a tumour.
mechanisms.explain: To spread, a tumour cell drops its junctions and becomes mobile (epithelial–mesenchymal transition, driven by SNAI1, TWIST1, ZEB1), digests its surroundings (MMPs), and grows its own blood supply (VEGFA and its receptors). These are late steps; variants here matter more for how a cancer behaves than for whether it starts.

disease_explain: Open Targets ties these genes to cancer through human genetics (GWAS and inherited variants), but Gene Ontology places them on none of the cell's stages yet. Many are risk loci near a gene whose role is still unclear.

organs.name: Living and resting
organs.about: Most cells rest (G0) or grow (G1). Growth signals from outside decide whether a cell starts another round of division, and contact with its neighbours holds it in place.

organs.name: Copying and dividing
organs.about: The cell copies its DNA (S phase), prepares (G2) and splits into two daughter cells (mitosis, M). A round takes about a day in fast-dividing tissue.

organs.name: Checkpoints
organs.about: Gates before copying (G1/S), before dividing (G2/M) and during division (spindle) stop the cycle when DNA is damaged or chromosomes are not attached, until it is fixed.

organs.name: Toxins and damage
organs.about: Toxins, radiation and the cell's own oxygen use damage DNA. Enzymes neutralise toxins and oxidants, and repair systems fix the damage.

organs.name: Ageing
organs.about: Each division shortens the telomeres at the chromosome ends. Short telomeres or lasting damage put the cell into senescence: alive, but never dividing again.

organs.name: Death and clearance
organs.about: A cell too damaged to repair kills itself (apoptosis), and the immune system finds and kills cells that show abnormal proteins.

organs.name: Escape: cancer
organs.about: A cell that slips past checkpoints, repair, ageing and death keeps dividing. To spread it must also break loose from its neighbours and grow its own blood vessels.
